entry.summary: Visa waiver for ordinary Australian passports, up to 30 days for business, tourism, visiting family and friends, or transit, until 31 December 2026.
entry.pre_arrival: Electronic arrival card on the National Immigration Administration site or by QR code at entry.
entry.other: Australians have been refused entry; medical screening on arrival can include a blood sample. A full visa must be obtained before travel.
entry.next_check: Watch item cn-visa-waiver-2026: the waiver ends 31 December 2026 unless extended.

tourism.detail: The policy covers tourism for Australian ordinary-passport holders and currently permits multiple entries.
tourism.next: Recheck the policy end date and passport conditions shortly before departure.

meetings.route: 30-day visa-free business visit; M visa for a longer or visa-required trip
meetings.detail: Meetings, negotiations and commercial visits fit the published business purpose.
meetings.next: Carry a host invitation and keep service delivery outside the meeting-only brief.

conference.detail: Conferences and exhibitions are expressly named in the current visa-free policy.
conference.next: Keep registration, invitation, accommodation and onward travel together.

unpaid-speaking.route: Visa-free entry (30 days, until 31 December 2026) for exchange visits
unpaid-speaking.detail: Exchange visits and business are visa-free purposes; work isn't. An unpaid talk as part of an exchange fits; anything paid doesn't.
unpaid-speaking.next: Ask the Chinese Embassy if the host pays you.

paid-speaking.route: Host-sponsored short-term work approval plus Z visa
paid-speaking.detail: A paid lecture, advisory session or professional service generally fits short-term work rather than business attendance.
paid-speaking.next: Have the contracting host start the work-approval process before the Z application.

book-launch.route: Split rights meetings, cultural appearance, speaking fee and retail sales
book-launch.detail: Publisher and rights meetings can fit business entry; a non-commercial appearance may fit exchange; paid delivery or personal sales change the route.
book-launch.next: Use a Chinese publisher or bookseller for local sales and classify the appearance separately.

ai-teaching.route: Short-term work approval and Z visa for up to 90 days
ai-teaching.detail: Paid technical, management or advisory teaching is treated as work; longer roles use the normal work-permit and residence process.
ai-teaching.next: Ask the university, company or event host to sponsor the exact teaching dates and duties.

remote-work.route: No dedicated national digital-nomad route identified
remote-work.detail: The current visa-free policy excludes people coming to work, and the official visa list has no remote-worker class.
remote-work.next: Map a city-specific residence or work route if China becomes a longer base.

entrepreneur.route: Business scouting first; city-specific entrepreneurship residence for a longer build
entrepreneur.detail: Foreigners can invest and establish enterprises subject to sector rules; Shanghai also publishes entrepreneurship residence pathways.
entrepreneur.next: Choose the city and entity role, then map investment approval separately from personal work status.

trade.route: 30-day visa-free business visit or M visa
trade.detail: Trade fairs, sourcing, negotiations and setup meetings fit the business lane.
trade.next: Separate negotiations from any local installation, operation or service delivery.

artist.route: Written exchange classification for non-commercial activity; cultural approval plus short-term employment approval plus Z visa for commercial performance
artist.detail: For a commercial performance of 90 days or less, the official short-work process requires both cultural-authority documents and short-term employment approval before the Z route.
artist.next: Have the promoter classify the engagement and coordinate all cultural, employment and visa documents.

mixed-mission.detail: Business, tourism and exchange parts fit; work, study or reporting parts need a visa.

filming.route: Journalist (J) visa or the right visa, not visa-free entry
filming.detail: Visa-free entry doesn't cover news coverage; reporting needs a journalist visa.
filming.next: Apply through the Chinese Embassy with the host's paperwork.

research.route: Visa-free entry (30 days, until 31 December 2026) for exchange visits
research.detail: Academic exchange visits are covered; paid research or study needs a visa.
research.next: Ask the Chinese Embassy if it's paid or long.

volunteering.route: Ask the Embassy of the People's Republic of China, Yarralumla
volunteering.detail: No official statement on this activity was read. Easy entry isn't permission to work.
volunteering.next: Ask the Embassy of the People's Republic of China, Yarralumla which visa covers it, in writing.

laws.rule: China has the death penalty for drug offences and other serious crimes. Under Chinese criminal law, it's possible for espionage and other national security offences to attract serious penalties, from lengthy custodial sentences to the death penalty. If you're sentenced to death, it's unlikely that Chinese authorities will grant you leniency.
laws.heading: Death penalty

laws.rule: Penalties for all types of drug offences including use, possession, manufacturing, selling or trafficking are severe and include life in prison or the death penalty. Authorities strictly enforce these laws, even for small quantities of 'soft' drugs, such as marijuana. These laws and severe penalties also apply to minors. Authorities conduct random drug tests, including at airports and on arrival to China. Police raids on nightclubs and bars frequented by foreigners can occur, with patrons subjected to urine and / or hair tests. A positive drug test can result in fines, detention and deportation, regardless of when or where the drugs were used. Authorities have executed foreigners for drug of
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Authorities may not allow you to leave China if you're involved in a: criminal matter or investigation civil or commercial dispute
laws.heading: Legal proceedings and investigations

laws.rule: Chinese authorities may place an exit ban upon an individual to prevent them from leaving the country. Sometimes, people only become aware of an exit ban when they try to leave China. Exit bans can be applied for a number of reasons, including if you're involved in legal proceedings in China. Exit bans can affect you even if you're not directly involved in the legal proceedings. Authorities have stopped some Australians from leaving China because of a dispute involving family members. Sometimes it's years before authorities allow people to leave China. Our ability to assist you if you're subject to an exit ban is limited. If you're involved in local legal matters: get professional advice you
laws.heading: Exit bans

laws.rule: China has strict laws on national security, which it updates from time to time. This includes laws that may punish individuals or organisations it considers to have engaged in activities that undermine ethnic unity and progress, create division, or incite separatism. These laws can be interpreted broadly and applied expansively and harshly. They may apply to online activity, public comments, publications, associations or other conduct. Penalties may be severe. Chinese authorities may define certain behaviours and activities as endangering national security that would not be considered as such in Australia. This could include activities that occurred outside of China. Authorities have detaine
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: China limits access to many foreign websites and social media services. You may be unable to access your banking, use popular phone apps, or make calls or send messages using internet-based services. The use of services to bypass local internet restrictions may be illegal and can attract penalties, including imprisonment. Mobile and internet service providers can be requested to provide data to Chinese authorities.
laws.heading: Internet access

laws.rule: Under Chinese law, you must register your place of residence with the local Public Security Bureau. You must do this within 24 hours of arriving and each time you change your residential location. An online registration system is available for the provinces of Hebei, Liaoning, Zhejiang, Hubei, Guangxi, Chongqing, and Sichuan. If you stay at a hotel, the staff do this as part of the standard check-in process. If you're staying elsewhere, such as with family or friends, visit the nearest police station. Present your passport and a valid Chinese visa. You must always carry identification and show it to the police if they ask for it. Authorities will accept your passport or a Chinese residence c
laws.heading: Registration and identification

laws.rule: Homosexuality is not illegal in China but be aware of local sensitivities, including with regards to public displays of affection. Chinese law doesn't guarantee freedom from discrimination for LGBTQIA+ travellers. Travellers whose gender expression or appearance may not align with the gender recorded in their passport may experience additional or intrusive questions from immigration authorities.
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ laws

laws.rule: You can only participate in religious activities at registered or approved locations. There are restrictions on foreigners organising or hosting religious services and associating with unapproved religious groups. Foreign nationals may invite Chinese religious professionals to perform ceremonies such as baptisms, weddings and funerals. Only foreigners may participate in religious events which are organised or hosted by foreigners. Permission should be obtained from the relevant religious affairs administration office that covers the event location.
laws.heading: Religious activities

laws.rule: China has experienced higher numbers of commercial disputes involving Australians in recent years. Before starting business relationships: investigate the market get professional advice conduct appropriate due diligence Get professional legal advice before entering into any contract in China. This includes residential leases and business contracts.
laws.heading: Doing business in China

laws.rule: Many business issues that Australians consider to be civil or commercial are classified as criminal matters in China. This is especially the case if state enterprises or state assets are involved. Penalties for commercial and economic crimes are often severe. Foreigners have been held against their will at their workplace. These incidents involved other companies or employees trying to resolve business and employment disputes.
laws.heading: Business versus criminal matters

laws.rule: Disputes over working and living conditions for Australians working in China are common. This is particularly the case for those teaching English. If you’re considering travel to China for work: verify the true nature of the work on offer make sure you have the correct visa before you arrive Authorities can fine or detain you if you don't maintain a valid visa. Get professional legal advice before signing any contract in Australia or China. Carefully check local laws about business or other activities you wish to undertake in China. laws.heading: Employment in China

laws.rule: You must hold a valid Chinese driver's licence or a temporary driving permit to drive. Foreign driver's licences and International Driving Permits (IDP) aren't valid in mainland China. You can apply for a Chinese driver's licence or a temporary driving permit at a local Vehicle Management Office or service centre. money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The currency in China is the Renminbi (RMB). Chinese law limits the amount of foreign currency you can carry in and out of China. If you’re entering China with more than RMB 20,000 (USD 5,000) or the same amount in any other currency, you must declare it to customs on arrival. Keep the declaration. You need to show it to customs officials when you leave. If you plan to leave China carrying more than RMB 20,000 (USD 5,000) or the same amount in another currency, you need permission from a Chinese bank.
